etymology: From Latin cratis, a hurdle or wickerwork, through Old French; a framework of crossed bars. In the tabernacle it renders Hebrew mikbar (H4345), from a root meaning to interweave or plait — the brasen lattice of the altar of burnt offering.
biblical_def: The grate is the “grate of network of brass” commanded for the altar of burnt offering (Exo 27:4), a brasen lattice set within the hollow altar, reaching to the midst of it beneath the compass (Exo 38:4). Bezaleel made it, and cast four rings for the four ends of the grate to be places for the staves (Exo 38:5); it is numbered among the vessels of the altar with his staves and all his instruments (Exo 35:16). This was no ornament but the working heart of the altar — the grating on which the fire burned and the sacrifice was consumed, the ashes falling through its network. Every lamb, every bullock, every whole burnt offering that ascended to the LORD passed through the fire that this brasen grate upheld. Brass throughout the sanctuary bears the weight of judgment and the endurance of fire; the grate is that which stands in the flame and does not fail. It is a fit and sober figure of the cross, where the true Sacrifice was laid in the fire of divine wrath and consumed in the sinner’s stead, yet the altar held. The grate teaches that acceptable worship is costly, fiery, and bloody — that sin is not waved away but burned away upon an altar God Himself appointed. The whole apparatus of network and rings and staves says that the way to God is by sacrifice, borne on the shoulders of an ordained priesthood, kindled with fire that the LORD would not let go out.
webster_summary: A framework of parallel or crossed bars; in the tabernacle, the brasen network within the altar of burnt offering.
webster_full: GRATE, noun. A partition, lattice, or frame of parallel or crossed bars, used to shut a passage while admitting sight or air, or to hold fuel above a hollow.
An instrument of iron or brass with bars or ribs, for holding fuel while fire burns beneath and ashes fall through.
In Scripture, the brasen grate of network made for the altar of burnt offering, set beneath the compass unto the midst of it (Exo 27:4; 38:4).
A frame of latticework covering an opening in a wall or window.
By extension, any reticulated or interwoven barrier of bars.

Exo 38:4

Exo 38:5
And he cast four rings for the four ends of the grate of brass, to be places for the staves.
The altar of burnt offering, with his brasen grate, his staves, and all his vessels, the laver and his foot,
corruption_summary: A vessel of the altar, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the costly, fiery nature of atonement against an age that wants forgiveness without a sacrifice.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the grate rebukes is the modern craving for a bloodless religion — a God who accepts without an altar, who pardons without a substitute, who warms the hands without kindling the fire. The brasen network standing in the flame is a standing witness that sin is dealt with by consuming judgment, and that the worshipper draws near only over a burnt offering. To forget the grate is to forget that mercy cost blood.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What must be recovered is reverence for the altar itself — the sober knowledge that the fire which burned upon that brasen grate was the LORD’s own appointment, and that the cross to which it pointed was no accident but the ordained furnace in which our Sacrifice was consumed. Recover the altar and you recover the seriousness of sin and the wonder of the blood that answers it.
roots_summary: Hebrew mikbar (H4345), a network or grating, from kabar to interweave; the brasen lattice of the altar.

No worshipper reached the mercy seat but by the altar whose grate stood in the fire of judgment.

etymology: Old English net joined to weorc, work — work in which threads or bars are crossed and knotted at intervals. In the sanctuary it renders Hebrew sebakah (H7639) and mikbar (H4345), the reticulated brass of pillar and altar.
biblical_def: Network is any fabric of crossed and knotted work, and in Scripture it names two ornaments of holy things wrought in brass. First, the altar of burnt offering was given a “grate of network of brass” (Exo 27:4), a reticulated lattice to bear the fire. Second, the two great pillars Jachin and Boaz before Solomon’s temple were crowned with chapiters covered by “two rows round about upon the one network” (1Ki 7:18), and Jeremiah, recording the fall of Jerusalem, lingers over these same pillars: “with network and pomegranates upon the chapiters round about, all of brass” (Jer 52:22), counting “ninety and six pomegranates on a side; and all the pomegranates upon the network were an hundred round about” (Jer 52:23). That the Spirit numbers the very pomegranates upon a doomed pillar teaches that God takes account of the beauty of His house even as He judges His people’s sin. The network is intricate, ordered, patient work — nothing careless, nothing thrown together. It rebukes the slapdash spirit that would serve God with the leftovers of attention. The interlaced brass, upholding fruit and enduring fire, quietly figures the Church, a body knit and framed together, many members joined and bearing fruit, standing in judgment’s heat by the strength of the God who wrought her. Where the world sees mere ornament, the eye of faith reads the diligence and order that reverence owes to the LORD.
webster_summary: Reticulated work in which bars or threads cross and knot at intervals; the brass lattice of altar and temple pillar.
webster_full: NETWORK, noun. A fabric or structure of threads, wires, or bars crossed at regular intervals and knotted or fastened at the crossings, leaving open interstices between.
Any system of lines, passages, or parts that cross and intersect after the manner of a net.
In Scripture, the brasen grate of network for the altar of burnt offering (Exo 27:4).
The reticulated brass covering the chapiters of the pillars Jachin and Boaz before Solomon’s temple (1Ki 7:18).
Ornamental latticework, especially of metal, upon a sacred or public structure.

corruption_summary: An ornament of God’s house, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the diligence and order that reverence owes, against an age content with careless worship.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the network rebukes is haste and carelessness in the things of God — the notion that He is served well enough by the hurried and the half-attentive. The Spirit who counted the very pomegranates upon a fallen pillar does not overlook whether we bring Him our diligence or our dregs. The intricate, knotted, patient brass is a standing reproof to slovenly worship and thrown-together devotion.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the beauty of order in the house of God — that the LORD is a God of intricacy and care, who framed His sanctuary with reticulated work bearing fruit, and who is honored when His people serve Him with the same ordered diligence rather than the leftovers of a distracted heart.

etymology: From Old French soc, a ploughshare, through a diminutive form — a hollow into which something is set. In the tabernacle it renders Hebrew eden (H134), a base or pedestal, the silver footings into which the boards were set.
biblical_def: The sockets are the silver bases of the tabernacle, hollowed pedestals into which the tenons of the upright boards were set to hold them fast. Forty sockets of silver stood under the twenty boards of a side, “two sockets under one board for his two tenons” (Exo 26:19), and so around the house, sixteen sockets under the eight boards of the west end (Exo 26:25), the whole standing on silver (Exo 26:21). The weight of this doctrine lies in the silver’s origin: “of the hundred talents of silver were cast the sockets of the sanctuary, and the sockets of the vail; an hundred sockets of the hundred talents, a talent for a socket” (Exo 38:27). That silver was the atonement money, the half-shekel ransom every man paid for his soul when he was numbered (Exo 30:12-16). So the entire tabernacle — every board of it — rested upon the redemption price of the people. The house of God stood on ransom silver; the sanctuary had atonement for its very foundation. Here is the gospel cast in metal: the whole habitation of God among men is founded upon a price paid to redeem souls, a talent of silver under every board. The Church of the living God rests on no other footing than the ransom of blood, the redemption not with corruptible things as silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ. Take away the sockets and the boards fall; take away redemption and there is no dwelling of God with man.
webster_summary: A hollow into which something is fitted; in the tabernacle, the silver bases cast of the atonement money to hold the boards.
webster_full: SOCKET, noun. A hollow or cavity into which anything is fitted, set, or inserted so as to be held fast.
The hollow of a candlestick or lamp into which the light is set.
In the tabernacle, a cast base or pedestal of silver, hollowed to receive the tenons of the boards (Exo 26:19).
A hundred such sockets were cast of a hundred talents of silver, a talent to each, from the atonement money of the numbered people (Exo 38:27).
By extension, any receiving hollow, as the socket of a bone, an eye, or a tool.

corruption_summary: A foundation of the sanctuary, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the truth that God’s dwelling rests wholly upon a paid redemption.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the sockets rebuke is the dream of a religion with no ransom — a fellowship with God resting on human sincerity, effort, or worth rather than a price paid for the soul. The silver under every board declares that not one part of the sanctuary stood on anything but atonement money. To imagine communion with God apart from redemption is to build boards with no sockets, a house with no foundation, which the first wind of judgment overthrows.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the whole habitation of God among His people rests upon redemption — a talent of ransom silver beneath every board. The Church stands on the blood of Christ and nothing else; her foundation was bought, and every believer set into that house is held fast by a price already paid.

etymology: Old English bord, a plank or table. In the tabernacle it renders Hebrew qeresh (H7175), an upright plank or board of shittim wood overlaid with gold, forming the standing walls of the sanctuary.
biblical_def: The boards are the standing walls of the tabernacle: planks of shittim wood, ten cubits high and a cubit and a half broad, set upright side by side to form the house of God. “Thou shalt make boards for the tabernacle of shittim wood standing up” (Exo 26:15), and Bezaleel “made boards for the tabernacle of shittim wood, standing up” (Exo 36:20). That thrice-noted posture — standing up — is not incidental; the boards do not lie flat as a floor to be trodden but rise erect as walls to enclose the holy things. Each was overlaid with gold, and given rings of gold for the bars that ran through them to bind the whole into one (Exo 26:29), and Moses at the last “set up the boards thereof” when he reared the tabernacle (Exo 40:18). The boards were of the wilderness acacia — a lowly, thorny desert tree — yet overlaid with pure gold and set upon silver sockets of redemption. Here is the believer figured: taken from the barren ground of nature, cut, planed, and stood upright, overlaid with a glory not his own, joined by golden bars to his fellows, and set fast upon a bought foundation. No board stood alone; each was bound to the next, and all rested on silver. The sanctuary was not a heap of timber but a framed and standing house, every plank in its place, every one clothed in gold, every one held together in one dwelling for God.
webster_summary: Upright planks; in the tabernacle, the gold-overlaid boards of shittim wood standing up to form the walls.
webster_full: BOARD, noun. A piece of timber sawn thin and broad; a plank of more than usual breadth used for building, flooring, or wall.
In the tabernacle, an upright plank of shittim wood, ten cubits high, overlaid with gold, forming the standing wall of the sanctuary (Exo 26:15).
A table; hence, that which is spread upon a table, provision, entertainment.
A council or authorized assembly seated at a table for business.
By extension, any broad, flat, thin surface of wood or like material.

And thou shalt overlay the boards with gold, and make their rings of gold for places for the bars: and thou shalt overlay the bars with gold.
And Moses reared up the tabernacle, and fastened his sockets, and set up the boards thereof, and put in the bars thereof, and reared up his pillars.
corruption_summary: The framing timber of the sanctuary, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the believer set upright, gilded, and joined into one house of God.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the boards rebuke is the modern love of the solitary and the self-standing — the notion that a man may be a believer alone, unbound to the fellowship, a plank refusing the bars that join him to his brethren. No board stood by itself in the tabernacle; each was bored for the bars and knit to the next, and all rested on common silver. The lone plank, unbound, is not the strength it imagines but a wall waiting to fall.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the desert acacia is cut, stood upright, overlaid with a glory not its own, and framed together with its fellows into one dwelling for God. The believer is not saved to stand alone but to be jointed by golden bars into the standing house, resting on the bought foundation, clothed in a righteousness supplied from above.

etymology: Plural of staff, Old English staef, a rod or pole. In the sanctuary it renders Hebrew bad (H905), a pole or bar; the shittim-wood carrying poles overlaid with gold or brass by which the ark and altars were borne.
biblical_def: The staves are the carrying poles of the holy vessels: rods of shittim wood, overlaid according to their vessel — gold for the ark and the golden things, brass for the altar of burnt offering. “Thou shalt make staves of shittim wood, and overlay them with gold” for the ark (Exo 25:13); and for the brasen altar, “staves of shittim wood, and overlay them with brass” (Exo 27:6). These were thrust through rings on the sides of each vessel, that the holy things might be borne on the shoulders of the Levites and never touched by the hand: Bezaleel “put the staves into the rings by the sides of the ark, to bear the ark” (Exo 37:5). The most searching word about the staves comes at Solomon’s temple, when the ark was set in the oracle: “they drew out the staves, that the ends of the staves were seen out in the holy place before the oracle… and there they are unto this day” (1Ki 8:8). The staves were drawn out but never removed — the ark had come to its rest, yet its pilgrim poles remained, their ends visible, a token that the God who had journeyed with His people in the wilderness was the same enthroned in Zion. The staves preach that the holy things are borne, not dragged; carried on consecrated shoulders, not handled by profane hands; and that even in rest the marks of the pilgrimage abide. The Church too is borne through her wilderness by an appointed ministry, her ark carried toward a rest where the pilgrim poles, though drawn out, are never taken away.
webster_summary: Carrying poles; in the sanctuary, the shittim-wood staves overlaid with gold or brass by which the ark and altars were borne.
webster_full: STAVES, noun. Plural of staff; rods, poles, or bars, especially such as are used for carrying a burden between them.

The staves of the ark were borne on the shoulders of the Levites, that the ark be not touched by the hand (Exo 37:5).
At the temple the staves were drawn out but not removed, their ends seen before the oracle (1Ki 8:8).
By extension, the bars or rundles of a ladder, or the wooden strips forming a cask.

corruption_summary: The carrying poles of the holy vessels, not a contested doctrine; they recover the reverent, shoulder-borne handling of holy things and the abiding marks of pilgrimage.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the staves rebuke is the profane, familiar handling of holy things — the hand laid on the ark that God said must be borne, the presumption that would carry the things of God on a new cart of human convenience rather than on consecrated shoulders. Uzzah’s fall stands as the warning. The staves teach that reverence is not optional decoration but the appointed manner of approach, and that the LORD will be sanctified in them that come nigh Him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is twofold: that the holy things are borne on consecrated shoulders and never grasped by profane hands, and that even in rest the pilgrim poles remain — drawn out, never removed. The people at rest in Zion still bore the tokens of the wilderness march, a witness that the God of the journey and the God of the rest are one.

etymology: From French tenon, from tenir, to hold, Latin tenere — a projecting tongue cut on the end of a timber to be held in a corresponding hollow. In the tabernacle it renders Hebrew yad (H3027), a hand, the projecting hands of the boards set into the silver sockets.
biblical_def: The tenons are the projecting tongues cut at the foot of each tabernacle board, by which the board was set fast into its silver sockets. “Two tenons shall there be in one board, set in order one against another: thus shalt thou make for all the boards of the tabernacle” (Exo 26:17); and Bezaleel wrought accordingly, “one board had two tenons, equally distant one from another” (Exo 36:22). The Hebrew calls them hands — each board had two hands reaching down into the redemption-silver of the sockets, gripping the foundation. Two occurrences only, yet the doctrine is weighty: the tenon is the point of union, the joint where the standing board is fitted to the bought base and to the framed whole. Nothing in the sanctuary was left loose or merely leaned; every board was joined, morticed, held. This is the very figure the apostle draws for the Church: “in whom all the building fitly framed together groweth unto an holy temple in the Lord” (Eph 2:21). The tenons are the fitting-together, the mortise-and-hand by which stone is knit to stone and member to member. A believer is not a plank leaning against the house but a board morticed into it, his two hands laid hold upon the redemption beneath, his sides bound to his brethren, growing up together into a holy temple. The whole strength of the tabernacle lay in its joints; and the whole strength of the Church lies in her being framed together in Christ, no member independent, every one fitted, every one held.
webster_summary: The projecting tongue on a timber’s end that enters a socket; in the tabernacle, the two hands of each board set into its silver bases.
webster_full: TENON, noun. The end of a piece of timber cut into a projecting tongue, to be inserted into a socket or mortise made to receive it, that the two may be firmly joined.
In the tabernacle, one of the two projecting tenons at the foot of each board, called in the Hebrew its hands (Exo 26:17).
Each board had two tenons, equally distant one from another, set into two silver sockets (Exo 36:22).
The instrument of union by which the standing boards were held fast to their bought foundation.
By extension, any joint in which a projecting part enters a corresponding cavity.
scriptures: Two tenons shall there be in one board, set in order one against another: thus shalt thou make for all the boards of the tabernacle.
One board had two tenons, equally distant one from another: thus did he make for all the boards of the tabernacle.
Eph 2:21
In whom all the building fitly framed together groweth unto an holy temple in the Lord:
And thou shalt make forty sockets of silver under the twenty boards; two sockets under one board for his two tenons, and two sockets under another board for his two tenons.
corruption_summary: The joints of the tabernacle boards, not a contested doctrine; they recover the fitting-together of God’s people, each member morticed into the whole.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the tenons rebuke is the spirit of the unjoined and the independent — the believer who would lean against the house without being morticed into it, the member who claims Christ but refuses to be fitted to His body. No board in the tabernacle merely leaned; each had its two hands reaching into the foundation and its sides bound to its fellows. The loose plank, unjoined, has no share in the strength of the framed house.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that all the building is “fitly framed together” (Eph 2:21) — that God’s people are not a heap of separate timbers but a temple morticed and knit, every member fitted, every one holding fast the redemption beneath and joined to those beside him, growing up together into an holy temple in the Lord.

etymology: Old English writhan, to twist or wreathe, joined to chain, from Latin catena. The wreathen chains are of Hebrew sharsherah (H8333), twisted or corded work; the plaited chains of pure gold that fastened the high priest’s breastplate.
biblical_def: The wreathen chains are the twisted cords of pure gold that bound the high priest’s breastplate of judgment to the ephod upon his shoulders. “Two chains of pure gold at the ends; of wreathen work shalt thou make them, and fasten the wreathen chains to the ouches” (Exo 28:14); “thou shalt make upon the breastplate chains at the ends of wreathen work of pure gold” (Exo 28:22); and they were put “in the two rings which are on the ends of the breastplate” (Exo 28:24), so that Bezaleel’s hands wrought them exactly (Exo 39:15). These were not loose chains but plaited, corded, wreathen — strength woven of many strands, that the breastplate bearing the twelve tribes’ names might never slip from the mediator’s heart. For upon that breastplate Aaron bore the names of the children of Israel over his heart when he went in before the LORD, and the wreathen chains are what held that memorial fast. Here the type shines: the names of God’s people are bound to the heart of the High Priest by golden cords that cannot be broken, plaited of a strength beyond the failing of any single thread. Our great High Priest bears His people’s names upon His heart within the veil, and no wreathen chain of grace shall part them from Him. The gold is pure, the work is corded, the fastening is sure — a figure of that love which many waters cannot quench, binding the redeemed to their Intercessor by links of everlasting strength.
webster_summary: Twisted or plaited cords; in the priesthood, the pure-gold wreathen chains that bound the breastplate to the ephod.
webster_full: WREATHEN, adjective. Twisted, wreathed, or plaited; made of strands wound together into a cord.
CHAIN, noun. A series of links or rings connected, used for binding, fastening, or ornament.
In the priesthood, chains of pure gold of wreathen or corded work, made for the ends of the breastplate (Exo 28:14).
Fastened to the ouches of the ephod and to the rings of the breastplate, binding it upon the high priest’s heart (Exo 28:22, 24).
By extension, any twisted ornamental cord-work of precious metal.

corruption_summary: The golden cords of the breastplate, not a contested doctrine; they recover the unbreakable binding of God’s people to the heart of their High Priest.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the wreathen chains rebuke is the fear that the believer’s union with Christ hangs by a single failing thread — that a slip of faith or a weight of sin might loose the breastplate from the mediator’s heart. But the chains were wreathen, plaited of many strands, of pure gold, fastened at both ends: strength upon strength. The doubt that God’s hold on His own is fragile is answered by the very make of these cords.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the security of the saints in their Intercessor. Our great High Priest bears His people’s names upon His heart within the veil, bound there by golden cords of covenant that cannot be broken. No wreathen chain of grace shall part the redeemed from the One who carries them before the throne.

etymology: From Old French lattis, from latte, a lath — a network of crossed laths or bars forming a screen over a window. It renders Hebrew eshnab (H822) and charak (H2762), the pierced or netted window-screen of an eastern house.
biblical_def: The lattice is the crossed screen of laths or bars set over an eastern window, through which one looked out or was glimpsed within, half-seen and half-hid. Scripture uses it in three scenes of watching and being watched. First, the mother of Sisera “looked out at a window, and cried through the lattice, Why is his chariot so long in coming?” (Jdg 5:28) — a heathen mother straining through the screen for a son who lay slain, a picture of vain hope peering after what will never return. Second, King Ahaziah “fell down through a lattice in his upper chamber” (2Ki 1:2) and, seeking Baalzebub rather than the LORD, died for it — the frail screen giving way, and the idolater falling through the very thing he leaned upon. But the third use lifts the word to glory: in the Song, the Bride says of her Beloved, “he standeth behind our wall, he looketh forth at the windows, shewing himself through the lattice” (Son 2:9). Here Christ is figured as One who, before the full unveiling, shews Himself through the lattice — giving His Church partial, tender, real glimpses of His face through the screen of ordinances, of Scripture, of providence, until the day the wall is taken down and we see Him face to face. The same crossed screen that framed a heathen mother’s vain watching and an idol-king’s deadly fall becomes, in the mouth of the Bride, the very lattice through which the Bridegroom lets His beloved catch sight of Him. What we now see through the lattice, we shall then see without a veil.
webster_summary: A window-screen of crossed laths or bars; the eastern lattice through which one looked out or was glimpsed within.
webster_full: LATTICE, noun. Any work of wood or metal made by crossing laths, rods, or bars, and forming open squares or lozenges between them.
A window or screen so made, admitting air and sight while veiling the interior.
In Scripture, the screen through which Sisera’s mother cried, watching for her son (Jdg 5:28).
The frail lattice through which Ahaziah fell to his death in Samaria (2Ki 1:2).
The lattice through which the Beloved sheweth Himself to His Bride (Son 2:9).

And Ahaziah fell down through a lattice in his upper chamber that was in Samaria, and was sick: and he sent messengers, and said unto them, Go, enquire of Baalzebub the god of Ekron whether I shall recover of this disease.
Son 2:9
My beloved is like a roe or a young hart: behold, he standeth behind our wall, he looketh forth at the windows, shewing himself through the lattice.
But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.
corruption_summary: A window-screen of the eastern house, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the sweet truth that Christ now shews Himself in part, until the veil is taken away.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the lattice rebukes is the twin error of despising the partial and demanding the total — either scorning the real glimpses of Christ granted through Word and ordinance because they are not yet the full vision, or, like Sisera’s mother, straining through the lattice after a false hope that will never come. Ahaziah leaned upon a frail screen and an idol and fell through both. The lattice teaches us to prize the true sight given now and to lean on the right object.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Bridegroom shews Himself through the lattice — that the Church’s present knowledge of Christ, though partial, is real and precious: we see now through a glass darkly, but then face to face (1Co 13:12). What is glimpsed through the screen of ordinances shall one day be beheld without a veil, when the wall is taken down and faith gives way to sight.

etymology: Probably from encasement, a hollow moulding or frame, related to case, from Latin capsa, a chest — a hinged window-frame or latticed opening. It renders Hebrew eshnab (H822), the pierced window-screen; a hapax legomenon in the KJV at Proverbs 7:6.
biblical_def: Casement appears but once in the KJV, in the seventh chapter of Proverbs, where the wise man sets himself as a watcher: “For at the window of my house I looked through my casement” (Pro 7:6). From that lattice he beholds among the simple ones a young man void of understanding, passing through the street near the corner of the strange woman’s house in the twilight, and going after her “as an ox goeth to the slaughter” until a dart strike through his liver. The casement is the vantage of watchful wisdom, the framed opening through which the discerning eye observes the folly and ruin of the careless. Scripture often sets a watcher at such a window: Abimelech “looked out at a window, and saw… Isaac was sporting with Rebekah” (Gen 26:8); Michal “looked through a window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before the LORD… and she despised him in her heart” (2Sa 6:16); and the Beloved “looketh forth at the windows, shewing himself through the lattice” (Son 2:9). The window is a place of seeing, and what a heart sees there reveals the heart itself — the wise man reads a warning, Michal reads only contempt, the Beloved offers a gracious sight. Through his casement the sage teaches by observation: he takes the ruin of a fool for a lesson, that we might learn wisdom at another’s cost and not our own. Blessed is the man who watches at wisdom’s casement, keeping his feet from the strange woman’s door because he has seen, through the lattice, where that road ends.
webster_summary: A window-frame or latticed opening that swings on hinges; the casement through which the wise man watched.
webster_full: CASEMENT, noun. A window, or part of a window, opening upon hinges; a hollow frame or moulding for a window.
A latticed or framed opening in a wall through which one may look out or in.
In Scripture, the casement of the wise man’s house, through which he beheld the simple young man going to ruin (Pro 7:6).
A hapax legomenon in the KJV, occurring only at Proverbs 7:6, rendering the Hebrew for a latticed window.
By extension, any frame that encloses or a hollow moulding, as in architecture.

corruption_summary: A latticed window of the eastern house, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the watchful wisdom that learns from another’s ruin.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the casement rebukes is heedlessness — the refusal to watch, to observe, to learn wisdom at another’s cost. The young man of Proverbs 7 was void of understanding because he did not see where his path led; the wise man at his casement did see, and set it down for our warning. An age that scorns instruction and must touch every fire for itself has forgotten the grace of learning through a watchful window rather than through one’s own destruction.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is watchful wisdom — the discipline of observing the ways of folly and the ends of sin, and taking warning before the dart strikes through the liver. Scripture sets a watcher at the window that we might learn to keep our own feet from the strange woman’s door, saved from ruin by a lesson seen and heeded rather than suffered.

etymology: Old English tange, a gripping instrument, from a root meaning to bite or seize. In the sanctuary it renders Hebrew melqachayim (H4457), from laqach, to take — the golden snuffers or tongs by which the priest handled the coals and wicks of the candlestick.
biblical_def: The tongs are the golden gripping-instruments of the sanctuary, made for the candlestick that its lamps might be dressed and its coals handled without a hand touching the fire. “The tongs thereof, and the snuffdishes thereof, shall be of pure gold” (Exo 25:38); they were covered with the candlestick under a cloth of blue when the camp journeyed (Num 4:9); and Solomon made them again for the temple, “the tongs of gold” before the oracle (1Ki 7:49). Small vessels, easily overlooked, yet of pure gold, for nothing that served the light of God’s house might be common. But the tongs rise to their highest use in the vision of Isaiah, where a seraph takes a live coal from off the altar “with the tongs” (Isa 6:6) and lays it upon the mouth of the trembling prophet, saying, “thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged” (Isa 6:7). Here the humble tongs become the very instrument of cleansing. No hand, not even a seraph’s, bears the altar-fire bare; the coal of atonement is carried by an appointed instrument to the unclean lips of a man undone. Here is the gospel in a golden tool: the fire that would consume the sinner, brought instead in mercy from the altar to purge him, applied by a hand not his own. The believer’s cleansing comes from the altar — from the sacrifice — and is laid upon him by a Mediator’s ministry, that the same fire which is judgment to the impenitent becomes to the contrite the very touch that takes away sin.

corruption_summary: A golden tool of the sanctuary, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the gospel of cleansing — altar-fire borne in mercy to purge the unclean.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the tongs rebuke is the contempt for small and appointed things — the notion that God’s cleansing might be seized directly, on our own terms, without the altar, the sacrifice, or the ordained means. But no hand bore the coal bare; even the seraph took it with the tongs. The sinner cannot snatch atonement; it is brought to him from the altar by a ministry not his own. To despise the means is to grasp at the fire and be consumed rather than cleansed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the gospel of cleansing shown in Isaiah’s coal: the fire that is judgment to the impenitent becomes, to the contrite, the very touch that takes away sin. The purging comes from the altar — from the Sacrifice — borne to unclean lips by a Mediator’s hand. “Thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged” is the word every trembling Isaiah longs to hear.
